key_insight: An instantaneous generalized total-enthalpy similarity closes both mean and fluctuating velocity–temperature relations in compressible turbulent boundary layers, yielding a unified Reynolds analogy from first principles.
engineering_relevance: This provides a parameter-free way to estimate heat transfer from flow statistics across Mach numbers and wall thermal conditions, improving turbulence modeling for high-speed thermal design.
method: Extend the generalized Reynolds analogy from mean fields to instantaneous total enthalpy–velocity similarity
Derive the fluctuating temperature–velocity ratio using universality of streamwise energy fraction, production–dissipation balance, and cutoff-scale scaling
Recover the refined strong Reynolds analogy as a special case and interpret its fitted coefficient via universal constants
evidence_signal: The relation is validated against boundary-layer DNS data over multiple Mach numbers and wall thermal conditions, where the predicted ratio collapses to unity and matches the refined strong Reynolds analogy benchmark.
watch_item: The closure relies on universal constants and equilibrium assumptions, so performance may degrade in flows with strong non-equilibrium, separation, or noncanonical wall heating.
paper_title: Generalized Reynolds Analogy for Compressible Turbulent Boundary Layers: Unified Velocity-Temperature Relations from Mean to Fluctuating Field
